entries.subject: flate: precompute literal costs for findMatch (#1217)
entries.message:
flate: precompute literal costs for findMatch (#1217)

Backport of https://go.dev/cl/829570 (golang/go#81398).

When estimating the gain of a candidate match at level 9, findMatch
summed the literal code lengths of the whole match for every candidate
that was longer than the best so far, which cost about a tenth of the
encoding time.

Compute a cumulative literal cost array over the window once per
deflateLazy call, right after the literal encoder used for the estimate
is generated, so that the cost of any range is a subtraction. Also
hoist the hash chain fields into locals for the chain walk.

Unlike upstream, litBits is a lazily allocated slice rather than an
array in advancedState, so only level 9 writers pay the 256KB; levels
7 and 8 never generate the estimate tables.

findMatch took the gain path for d.chain >= 100 while deflateLazy only
generated the tables it needs for d.chain > 100. No level has a chain
of exactly 100 so this was unreachable, but the mismatch is now load
bearing (a nil litBits instead of a nil d.h), so the conditions are
made to agree.

bitLengthRaw is no longer used and is removed. The output is
byte-identical.

entries.subject: s2: arm64 assembly encoders, lowered from the amd64 avo program (#1187)
entries.message:
s2: arm64 assembly encoders, lowered from the amd64 avo program (#1187)

* s2, zstd: arm64 asm via avo lowering (NOT SHIPPABLE — see benchmarks)

Complete and correct, retained for reference only. Full s2 suite passes on
Neoverse N1; zstd encode tests pass. Measured against the pure-Go path arm64
used previously:

  s2 Twain default   -11.9% time (+13.6% B/s)
  s2 Twain better    -11.4%
  s2 snappy-default  -12.6%
  s2 Random 1MB default  +16% time
  s2 Random 1MB better  +156% time (-61% B/s)
  geomean            +8.7% SLOWER

  zstd matchLen      ~24% slower than generic Go at 1-8KB

Incompressible input emits one large literal run, so that benchmark is
essentially a memmove: Go's runtime memmove reaches ~11 GB/s on arm64 while
the generator's inlined 128-byte MOVOU loop manages ~4.6 GB/s. matchLen
loses for a related reason -- the x86 source keeps lengths in 32-bit
registers, costing MOVWU truncations, and Go compiles its generic
le.Load64/TrailingZeros64 loop more tightly than the lowered x86.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* s2: regenerate arm64 with improved printer (address caching, GOAMD64 evaluation)

Regenerated output only. Still not shippable per the benchmarks in the
previous commit; retained so the branch reflects the current printer.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* s2: regenerate arm64 against the current lowering

The previous arm64 generation no longer builds: the lowering has since
stopped interpreting preprocessor directives (that machinery produced
about a third of the miscompiles review found) and has grown a guard
against reading a carry flag across DECQ. Both fire on this generator.

Neither is really an arm64 question. The GOAMD64 blocks -- the v4-to-v3
promotion and the TZCNT/BSF selection -- are instructions to the amd64
assembler, so arm64 is emitted by a separate pass that omits them and
uses TZCNTQ outright, which lowers to RBIT+CLZ. Keeping the amd64 pass
untouched is also what keeps its output identical, and it is: byte for
byte against master, header and build tag aside.

The carry guard is pointing at something real. genMemMoveLong's loop
branches JA on the carry that a SUBQ two instructions earlier left,
because x86 DECQ deliberately preserves CF where the arm64 SUBS it
lowers to does not. The previous generation predates the guard and so
emitted that branch reading a flag its producer no longer set. arm64
now gets the same 32 bytes per iteration with the branch reading a CMPQ
that immediately precedes it.

Full s2 test suite passes on Neoverse-N1.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* zstd: drop the arm64 matchLen from this branch

It measured ~24% slower than the generic Go loop on Neoverse-N1 (8KB:
879ns lowered vs 706ns Go), which is the expected direction: the x86
source does its length arithmetic in 32 bits, costing truncations once
lowered, and Go's le.Load64-xor-TrailingZeros64 loop already compiles to
tighter arm64 than the translation of the x86 does.

It rode along on the branch this one descends from. It does not belong
in a change about the s2 encoders.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* s2: drop the GOAMD64 guard around TZCNT, per review

TZCNT's encoding is BSF's with an F3 prefix, and processors without the
instruction ignore the prefix and execute BSF. One encoding is therefore
correct everywhere, and the assembler-level choice this made was never
needed.

The two differ only on a zero input, which cannot reach here -- every
caller has established the value is nonzero -- and in flags, which is
unobservable: all seventy call sites are followed immediately by SARQ,
which overwrites the flags without reading them. Verified by scanning
the generated output: seventy sites, seventy SARQ successors, no
conditional jump within two instructions of any of them.

The amd64 output changes by exactly the seventy BSFQ lines and their
surrounding directives; the instruction stream is otherwise identical
modulo avo's operand alignment. arm64 output is unchanged -- it already
emitted TZCNTQ unconditionally, which is what prompted the question.

This removes the per-site GOAMD64 directives, leaving only the v4-to-v3
promotion block at the top of the file, so the arm64 pass still has to
be separate.

entries.subject: huff0: add arm64 assembly for Decompress4X/1X via avo lowering (#1172)
entries.message:
huff0: add arm64 assembly for Decompress4X/1X via avo lowering (#1172)

Generate arm64 asm from the existing avo source with the honeycombio/avo
arm64 lowering printer (-arch amd64,arm64), the same mechanism zstd's
seqdec/fse asm already uses. The amd64 output is unchanged.

The Go-side wrappers move to decompress_asm.go, shared between amd64 and
arm64; per-arch files keep only the asm stubs and dispatch (amd64 retains
the BMI2 selection for Decompress1X; arm64 lowers the generic twin).

The avo pin gains exact x86 partial-register semantics (MOVB/MOVW/ADDB/
ADCB/SETcc lower to bit-field inserts preserving untouched bits) — the
huff0 loops pack output bytes through AH and accumulate byte counters,
which the previous lowering silently corrupted — plus constant-folding of
BMI2 control registers (BEXTR with an adjacent constant control becomes a
single UBFX). zstd/seqdec_arm64.s is regenerated with the same printer;
its amd64 output is byte-identical to before.

On a 16-core Cortex-A72 (ARMv8.0), huff0 Decompress1X improves 25-34%
(twain 114->153 MB/s, digits 128->161 MB/s); Decompress4X is content-
dependent (+12% twain, -4% low-entropy). zstd DecodeAll improves 1-7%
end-to-end (urls.10K +3.8%, html +2.2%, comp-data.bin +6.6%), with
checksum (18% of CPU, at scalar xxhash roofline) and sequence decoding
dominating the remainder.

Validated: full huff0 + zstd test suites on arm64 (Cortex-A72) and amd64;
avo differential execution tests for every new/changed lowering on both
architectures.

entries.subject: huff0: reshape the Decompress4X asm loops around a sentinel bit container (#1209)
entries.message:
huff0: reshape the Decompress4X asm loops around a sentinel bit container (#1209)

* huff0: reshape the Decompress4X asm loops around a sentinel bit container

Rewrite the 4X main loops in the shape of zstd's HUF_decompress4X1 fast
loop. Each of the four streams keeps its bit container and output pointer
in a register across iterations; only the input pointers stay in memory,
touched once per reload. A sentinel bit sits just below the unread bits,
so the consumed count is a trailing-zero count and there is no bitsRead
register, no per-symbol fill branch, and no AL/AH byte packing of the
output (which lowered to BFI chains on arm64). Five symbols per stream are
decoded between reloads for tablelog 9..11 and seven for tablelog <= 8;
the reload is branch-free. Bounds are hoisted to an outer loop that bounds
iterations by both the output limit and the lowest input pointer, so every
read stays inside the block even for corrupt input.

The inner decode is 5 instructions per symbol on both amd64 and arm64
against roughly 9-11 before, and there is now a BMI2 twin on amd64.

The hand-off back to the Go tail loop is the delicate part. The asm returns
the sentinel container and a signed distance from the stream start; a
stream can legitimately end with its 8-byte window up to 7 bytes below its
own start (those bytes belong to the previous stream), and the sentinel is
ORed over the window's lowest data bit, so restoreFromAsm re-reads the
window from memory rather than trusting the register, exactly as reference
zstd does. prepareForAsm slides the window down a byte for streams whose
final byte is 0x01, which would otherwise start with 8 consumed bits and
let a full group shift the sentinel out.

Reloads use TZCNT in both twins: avo models BSF's destination as
read-write (undefined on zero input), which makes the temporary live
across the whole loop and overflows the register budget. TZCNT is a pure
write, and for the non-zero input the sentinel guarantees it runs as BSF
on pre-BMI1 CPUs.

Tests: unit tests for the two conversions, a no-BMI2 twin of the 4X
roundtrip test, and a no-BMI2 leg in FuzzCompress.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* huff0: add a 14-symbol 4X loop variant for tablelog <= 4

With one bit per symbol the fixed reload cadence of the 7-symbol loop
reloads every 7 bits where the old loop filled every 32, which showed up
as +4.7% on the two lowest-entropy benchmark cells on Sapphire Rapids (it
was still -39% on Neoverse N1). 14 symbols of at most 4 bits fit the same
56-bit budget, so this is the same generator with a third symbol count.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* huff0: keep the 4X loops' input pointers in explicit context fields

Go fills ctx.ip[i] and ctx.ilowest from the bit reader slices, the asm
advances ip, and off is written once in the epilogue as the signed
distance from the stream start. The loop keeps the context pointer as its
memory base instead of the reader array, which also removes the reload of
the context pointer from the stack on every inner iteration. No field
changes meaning while the call is in flight.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* huff0: bound 4X asm reads by the block start, not stream 0's start

The window may reach into the 6-byte jump table below stream 0, which is
inside src and already handled by restoreFromAsm as consumed bytes. This
keeps the asm running about six bytes longer per stream, which for streams
with very short codes (pngdata at ~1.1 bits/symbol, tablelog 1 inputs)
shrinks the Go tail from ~115 to ~70 symbols per stream and removes a
+9% regression on 10 KB inputs on Sapphire Rapids.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* huff0: bound the 4X asm output batch by the symbols per iteration

The outer loop divided the remaining output budget by 8 to get the number
of inner iterations it could run before re-checking bounds. That was only
valid while an iteration wrote at most 8 bytes per stream, which the
14-symbol tablelog <= 4 loop broke: a batch could advance the output
pointers 1.75x past the limit, and with corrupt input (streams whose read
pointers stay high, so the input bound never fires) stream 3 wrote past
the end of the output buffer before the Go tail reported the corruption.
Through zstd's literal buffer that is a heap overrun from untrusted input.
Found by review; valid input was not observed to trigger it but was not
proven safe either.

Divide the output budget by the next power of two at or above the symbol
count instead (5 and 7 -> 8, 14 -> 16), and make the generator panic if a
future symbol count does not fit its shift. Add a guard-byte test that

buffers with 4 KiB of canary after the capacity, on both amd64 twins; it

roundtrips under every table size with the output capacity exact (the
allocator's size classes otherwise hide small overruns from every other
test), an end-to-end case for streams whose final byte is 0x01 so the
window slide in prepareForAsm is exercised through the public API, a note
on the generic twins that avo's "Requires: BMI" stamp comes from TZCNT
which runs as BSF without BMI1, and a pointer from the Go-side limit
comment to where the batch bound lives.

entries.message:
zstd: bump avo pin, regenerate arm64 asm (#1167)

* zstd: bump avo pin, regenerate arm64 with BMI2 lowering

Bumps the pinned avo commit (honeycombio/avo) past today's fixes: a
flag-liveness bug and a 32-bit CMPL/TESTL fold bug (neither actually reachable
from this codebase - seqdec's generated output is byte-identical without
them, and CMPL/TESTL aren't used here at all), plus a new EQ/NE-only
sub-32-bit CMPW/TESTB lowering that fse_decoder's buildDtable needs.

Checked whether the sub-word compare/test fold (the general form of which the
new avo now refuses to lower) actually produced wrong output in the
already-shipped fse_decoder_arm64.s: it didn't. All three call sites happened
to operate on registers already clean above the compared width (via an
upstream sign/zero-extending load, or a preceding bounds check), verified by
tracing register provenance by hand. Real risk, but mitigated by accident
rather than by design - which is exactly why the stricter check is worth
having going forward.

The new avo also prefers the BMI2 twin over the generic one when lowering to
arm64 (arm64 has native flag-free equivalents for the BMI2 idioms), so
seqdec_arm64.s now lowers sequenceDecs_decode_bmi2/decodeSync_bmi2 instead of
the generic variants. Symbol names are unaffected (arm64Name strips the
_bmi2/_amd64 suffix either way).

Validated: go vet and go test ./zstd/... pass natively on arm64; FuzzDecodeAll
(26.4M execs), FuzzDecoder (9.6M execs), and FuzzDecAllNoBMI2 pass with zero
crashers.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* zstd: bump avo pin, prefer generic (non-BMI2) twin on arm64

Benchmarking the BMI2-preferred seqdec on real hardware (Apple M4, Cortex-A72)
showed it's 13-50% slower than the generic twin, not faster as assumed -- see
the follow-up avo commit for why. Bump past that fix; avo's arm64 lowering now
defaults to the generic twin (ARM64PreferBMI2 defaults false), which this repo
doesn't override. seqdec_arm64.s is now byte-identical to what #1160 shipped,
aside from the skip-reason comment text; fse_decoder_arm64.s is unchanged
(the CMPW/TESTB fix has no BMI2 twin to choose between).

I have taken the experiences from this library and created a backwards compatible compression package called MinLZ.

That package will seamlessly decode S2 content, making the transition from this package fairly trivial.

entries.message:
gzhttp: Add zstandard to server handler wrapper (#1121)

Both gzip and zstd compression are now enabled by default. When a client supports both, zstd is preferred due to its better compression ratio and speed.

Zstd compression is enabled by default alongside gzip. When the client supports both, zstd is preferred because it typically offers better compression ratios and faster decompression.

The server uses `Accept-Encoding` header negotiation to select the best encoding:
- If client only accepts `gzip` → response is gzip compressed
- If client only accepts `zstd` → response is zstd compressed
- If client accepts both with equal qvalues → zstd is used (configurable)
- If client specifies qvalues (e.g., `gzip;q=1.0, zstd;q=0.5`) → higher qvalue wins

Default zstd settings are conservative for broad compatibility:
- Level: `SpeedFastest` (1) - maximum speed
- Window size: 128KB - minimal memory usage
- Concurrency: 1 - single-threaded per request

128-bit moves now use FMOVQ, which takes a base+displacement operand
directly, where the previous VLD1/VST1 needed the address materialized into
a scratch register first. And scalar accesses fold base+index into the
instruction when arm64 permits it (the index shift must equal log2 of the
access width, and no displacement may be present), with a cache so a run of
accesses sharing a base and index computes the address once. x86 folds
base+index+displacement into a single instruction and the generators lean on
that heavily, so this recovers much of what the lowering used to pay per
access.

seqdec_arm64.s and decompress_arm64.s together shed about 90 lines. The
amd64 assembly is byte-identical.

Measured on Neoverse N1 (Ampere, go1.26, -count 6, every result p<0.03):

  Decoder_DecodeAll geomean            -1.53%
    html.zst                           -2.29%
    plrabn12.txt.zst                   -2.19%
    lcet10.txt.zst                     -2.11%
    kppkn.gtb.zst                      -2.08%
    alice29.txt.zst                    -2.02%
  huff0 Decompress geomean             -0.81%
    Decompress4X/twain                 -2.81%

Inputs that are not sequence-bound (fireworks.jpeg, html_x_4) are unchanged,
as expected.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* zstd, huff0: bump the pinned avo to pick up thirteen lowering fixes

Generated output is unchanged -- regenerating against this pin reproduces
every .s file byte for byte, which also confirms none of the fixed bugs was
reachable from these generators. The pin still matters: it is what the next
regeneration uses.

Three review passes over the lowering found thirteen ways it could emit
plausible-looking but wrong arm64. About half are wrong values: byte extends
reading the wrong field from a high-byte source, a 32-bit conditional move
losing x86's unconditional zero-extension, a negative 32-bit immediate
sign-extending across all 64 bits, BEXTR clobbering its own staged control
field with a memory source, and compare/test/multiply loading eight bytes for
a four-byte memory operand, which can fault at a page boundary.

The rest are cases where the two architectures disagree about what a flag
means, and the lowering now refuses to translate rather than emit something
plausible: carry conditions after additions and after logical ops (both
invert), carry read across INC/DEC (which preserve it on x86 but not once
lowered), ADC after anything but a compare or subtract, a signed sub-word
compare whose consumer sits past a flag-transparent instruction, and the
XOR-self zeroing shortcut, which dropped the zero flag x86 sets there.

The last round also resolves the GOAMD64 conditionals before the flag
analyses run, so those see exactly the instructions that will be emitted --
otherwise a producer inside a dead arm could absorb a mark a live one needed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* zstd, huff0: narrow two table loads to MOVWQZX, and bump the pinned avo

The avo bump carries seven lowering fixes from a fourth review pass (see
the fork's log). One of them matters here: a 16-bit load into a register
lowered to a zero-extending arm64 load, where x86 preserves the upper 48
bits. Nothing in this repository was miscompiled by that -- at all forty
affected sites the destination's upper bits are dead, so zero-extending
was harmless as applied -- but the printer cannot know that, and an avo
program that did depend on those bits would have gotten wrong code.

Making the lowering exact costs an instruction on every 16-bit load, and
that instruction reads the destination it writes, which turns an
independent load in huff0's innermost decode loop into a loop-carried
dependency: measured +11.74% geomean on Decompress4X on Neoverse N1, up
to +19% (p=0.000, n=12). zstd's DecodeAll paid a smaller +0.73%.

So this asks for what the code actually wants. Every one of these sites
loads a table entry and then reads only its low bits, so none of them
needs the surrounding register preserved; MOVWQZX says that, and lowers
back to a single folded load. This is belt and suspenders -- there was no
bug here to fix -- it just keeps the general safety fix from costing
anything where preservation was never wanted.

It is also simply the better x86 encoding, which is worth having on its
own: MOVZX avoids the 66h operand-size prefix and the partial-register
merge dependency, the same hazard that cost 11.74% on arm64. On amd64
huff0 Decompress4X that is -7.59% geomean, up to -14.10% (p=0.000, n=12,
Ryzen 5 5600X).

Net effect on generated code: huff0/decompress_arm64.s and
zstd/seqdec_arm64.s are byte-identical to before, zstd/fse_decoder_arm64.s
loses two instructions to folded addressing, and the amd64 files pick up
the faster encoding. The two changes land together because the pin bump
alone would regress arm64 until the generators were narrowed.

* zstd, huff0: bump the pinned avo for the round-five lowering fixes

Generated assembly is unchanged, byte for byte. None of this round's
bugs was reachable from these generators: they emit only GOAMD64
directives, which the lowering resolves and removes, so the state that
was leaking across foreign preprocessor arms had nothing to leak past.
The pin moves anyway so the committed assembly corresponds to a printer
we would be willing to point at other code.

* zstd, huff0: bump the pinned avo for the round-six lowering fixes

Generated assembly is unchanged, byte for byte. The 64-bit immediate
sign-extension bug this picks up needs a Q-width immediate with bit 31
set, which neither of these generators emits -- s2's does, which is why
it was worth finding.

* zstd, huff0: bump the pinned avo for the round-seven lowering fixes

Generated assembly is unchanged, byte for byte. The frame-offset fix this
round originally carried landed separately as #1176 and is already in the
base; regenerating against this pin reproduces it exactly, which is the
check that the two arrived at the same answer rather than merely at
compatible ones.

Round seven's other fixes are not reachable from these generators: the
three-operand SHL/SHR forms are rejected (they are SHLD/SHRD, a different
instruction whose destination is the third operand); preprocessor
directives are normalized so "# else" is recognized, since Go's assembler
tokenizes the '#' separately and a missed #else drops BOTH arms; and the
mixed-comment check moved into the preprocessor evaluator, deleting a
second stateless opinion about directive ownership that had already
disagreed with the authoritative one.

* zstd, huff0: bump the pinned avo for the round-eight lowering changes

The address cache is gone from the lowering. It let a second access to
the same base and index reuse the register the first one computed, and
it had to be invalidated at every boundary the printer does not
otherwise model -- two of the silent miscompiles found in review were
missing invalidations rather than missing lowerings.

Measured here, it was worth two instructions: seqdec_arm64.s and
huff0/decompress_arm64.s are byte-identical without it, and
fse_decoder_arm64.s gains two ADDs in buildDtable, which runs once per
block. Most accesses fold base+index into the instruction and never
materialize an address at all, so there was rarely anything to cache.

Round eight's review found no new lowering bugs, so the rest is
housekeeping: dead code removed, a confusing panic given a real message.

* zstd, huff0: bump the pinned avo for the round-nine lowering fixes

Generated assembly is unchanged, byte for byte. None of round nine's
bugs is reachable from these generators: the CMN boundary case needs a
compare against INT32_MIN written as a signed immediate, and the two
directive-coupling holes need directives, which neither generator emits.

* zstd, huff0: bump the pinned avo for the round-ten and -eleven changes

Generated assembly is unchanged, byte for byte, including across the
removal of the lowering's preprocessor-directive support -- neither of
these generators emits a directive, which is most of why that support
was removed.

Also picks up shift counts at or above the operand width being masked
the way x86 masks them, rather than passing through to an arm64
immediate form that rejects them, and 64-bit immediates written unsigned
with the top bit set being read as the bit pattern amd64 wraps them to
rather than refused.

* zstd, huff0: bump the pinned avo for the round-eleven guard fixes

Generated assembly unchanged, byte for byte. Both fixes are to the guard
that refuses preprocessor directives, which neither of these generators
emits.

* zstd, huff0: bump the pinned avo for the round-twelve guard fixes

The only change to generated assembly is one build-tag line per file:
the original constraint is now bracketed before the arm64 term is
ANDed onto it. That is a no-op for these three -- every constraint here
is a pure AND chain -- but without it a constraint containing || would
have parsed as "(arm64 && ...) || ..." and pulled the arm64 assembly
into non-arm64 builds.

Instructions are byte-identical. Verified building and testing both
architectures.

* zstd, huff0: bump the pinned avo for the label-name guard

Generated assembly unchanged, byte for byte.

* zstd, huff0: bump the pinned avo for the round-thirteen hardening

Generated assembly unchanged, byte for byte. Round thirteen found no
miscompiles; the changes make flag transparency, instruction suffixes,
branch targets and the one-line output invariant into properties this
printer checks itself rather than ones that held because a separate tool
happened to reject the alternative.

* zstd, huff0: bump the pinned avo for the round-fourteen enforcement

Generated assembly unchanged, byte for byte. The lowering now checks both
directions of the flag contract at generation time: an instruction claimed
flag-neutral must emit no flag-writers, and one marked as a producer must
emit exactly one.

entries.subject: Refactor zstd decoder (#498)
entries.message:
Refactor zstd decoder (#498)

# TLDR;

* Streams can now be decoded without goroutines using `WithDecoderConcurrency(1)`.

* `WithDecoderConcurrency(4)` is now default. If you need more concurrent `DecodeAll` operations, use `WithDecoderConcurrency(0)`.

Goroutines exit when streams have finished reading (either error or EOF).

Designed and tested to be compatible, but test before committing upgrade.

# Changes

Goroutines will now only be created on demand, and `WithDecoderConcurrency(1)` is now strictly synchronized.

Decompression will typically be about 2x faster when using multiple goroutines, and will prepare input for the upstream reader async to reads. This can lead to ~3x faster input in total than using no goroutines.

New default is now `WithDecoderConcurrency(4)` (or less, if GOMAXPROCS is less). Beyond 4, there is little benefit for streaming decompression.

* No goroutines created, unless streaming, and auto-closed at error/EOF.
* Synchronous stream decoding with  `WithDecoderConcurrency(1)`.
* Split sequence decoding/execution for streams up to 50% faster.
* Simplified error flow.
* Speedup on streams.
* More consistent error reporting.
* Improved error detection/compliance with reference decoder.
* Improved test coverage.

Fixes #477

entries.subject: flate: avoid FMA in EstimatedBits for portable rounding (#1224)
entries.message:
flate: avoid FMA in EstimatedBits for portable rounding (#1224)

EstimatedBits and mFastLog2 had chained multiply-add expressions
that the compiler is allowed to contract into fused multiply-adds.
FMA contraction rounds differently than sequential multiply+add,
so EstimatedBits previously returned a different result on
architectures with hardware FMA (e.g. arm64) than on default amd64,
making EstimatedBits, and the resulting compressed output, GOARCH-dependent.

Fixes https://github.com/klauspost/pgzip/issues/72

entries.subject: Rewrite level 2+3+4 compression (#61)
entries.message:
Rewrite level 2+3+4 compression (#61)

* WIP: Rewrite level 2 compression

Rewrite level 1 to a new level 2, that can do cross-block matching.

Currently this is a rewrite of level 1 which allows us to retain the hash table between blocks. It is close to the same speed as level 1, but no previous block matching has been added.

* Implement level 2 (cross-block matches) and level 3 (2 checks per hash).

* Only check second candidate if value mismatches.

* Fine tune compression settings.

* Rebalance to adjust for new compression levels.

* For level 3, add another hash to the table before resuming.

* Adjustments to balance.

* Restore compressed content performance

* Fix flush/reset.

* Simplify offset handling for faster encoding.

* Also attempt to match first byte

* Initialize to maxStoreBlockSize to invalidate zero values.

* Revert test limit changes and tighten some.

* Add specialized level 4 which checks length of up to two candidates.

* Adjust level 4 limit.

* Eliminate bounds checks in match length.

Increases speed considerably on well-matching material.

entries.subject: zstd/huff0: pin avo peephole folds, regenerate arm64 (#1199)
entries.message:
zstd/huff0: pin avo peephole folds, regenerate arm64 (#1199)

Pulls in honeycombio/avo@0a52965 (branch lizf.arm64-peepholes): the
printer now folds "AND $mask x2 + TST" (x86's same-register TESTB/
TESTW idiom) to a single masked TST, and "MOVQ/SHRQ+MOVBQZX" self-
extends to a single UBFX. Regenerated amd64 output is byte-identical
(these are arm64-only printer changes); arm64 output shrinks by
exactly the matched sites: the loop-bottom exhausted-flag check in
both huff0 4X loops (3 insns -> 1) and the FSE table-build check, and
the "moB" byte extract in all four zstd seqdec_* functions (4 insns
-> 1, dropping a dead MOVD to RSP too).

Motivated by production pprof profiling (Honeycomb's arm64 Lambda
workload, Graviton2). Benchmarking to follow before deciding whether
this ships.

entries.subject: zstd/huff0: branch-free arm64 decode reads, avo shift-copy folds, whole-register 4X exhausted counter (#1203)
entries.message:
zstd/huff0: branch-free arm64 decode reads, avo shift-copy folds, whole-register 4X exhausted counter (#1203)

* zstd: branch-free length reads and fewer memory round trips in the asm decoders

Production arm64 profiles (Honeycomb's Lambda workload) put a quarter of
decompression time in sequenceDecs_decodeSync_arm64, spread over the
three extra-bits reads, the FSE state updates, and the loads and stores
that shuttle values through ctx and the frame. This reshapes the generic
(non-BMI2) generator path, which is what the arm64 lowering starts from,
without changing what any input decodes to.

Length reads (updateLength) lose their three branches. The generic path
tested addBits for zero and checked for overread before shifting;
neither branch is data-independent, and the offset one flips with every
repeat-offset sequence. The read is now (value<<bitsRead)>>1>>(63-n),
which is bitReader.get32BitsFast's value for every n the tables can
hold (addBits is at most 30) and 0 for n == 0, so it matches the Go
reference and the BMI2 twin, which never carried the checks: the fill
before each group of reads guarantees the bits, and a stream that runs
dry is reported at the next fill. The FSE state reads (getBits) take the
same shape in place of a rotate and a (1<<n)-1 mask build.

Memory traffic per sequence drops by two ctx dereferences per table
load, two per iteration-counter access, and the seqSize read-modify-
write: the table base pointers and the counter are copied to frame
slots at entry (the counter is written back to ctx on every exit of the
decode variants, where the caller reads it to locate a failing
sequence), and decodeSync recovers seqSize once at loop exit from the
outPosition delta, which is exactly the sum of ll+ml. The copy step
also takes ll, mo and ml from the registers the value checks already
hold instead of reloading the three slots.

On arm64 this removes 43 instructions from decodeSync's main loop as
generated, more on the executed path, with the remaining copies of the
shift count and source to be taken up by the lowering.

Validated: go vet on amd64 and arm64; zstd tests on amd64 including the
forced non-BMI2 runs; FuzzDecodeAll (5.4M execs, BMI2 versus generic
byte-identical) and FuzzDecAllNoBMI2 (9.2M execs); zstd tests on arm64
under qemu-user; and a digest of DecodeAll over all 10,091 corpus
entries identical between amd64 asm, amd64 noasm and arm64 asm.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_015dheXiuzL7dbQM3hjjS4zm

* zstd/huff0: bump avo, regenerate arm64 with the shift-copy folds

Pulls in honeycombio/avo@67bf513, whose arm64 lowering absorbs the
register copies x86's shift forms force: the count copy into CL and the
source copy before an in-place shift both disappear into arm64's
three-operand shifts where a straight-line scan proves the copy dead,
a SETcc into a freshly zeroed register becomes one CSET, and ADCQ $0
lowers to a single CSINC.

amd64 output is byte-identical; only the arm64 files change, by exactly
the matched sites: every peekTopBits in both huff0 4X loops (three
instructions to one LSR, eight per iteration of the 16-bit loop), the
exhausted-flag zero-and-set at the top of those loops, and the count and
source copies feeding the shifts in every zstd seqdec function and the
FSE table builder.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_015dheXiuzL7dbQM3hjjS4zm

* huff0: keep the 4X exhausted counter in a whole register

The four-stream decoders accumulate "this stream ran dry" in a byte:
XORL to clear, SETGE into the low byte, ADCB $0 per stream, TESTB at the
loop bottom. The count never exceeds five, so the full register serves
as well, and the byte-lane forms cost on both sides: on x86 a partial
write, on arm64 a bit-field insert after every CSET and CSINC because
the lowering must preserve the bits x86 would. With XORQ, ADCQ $0 and
TESTQ (SETcc has no wider form, but the lowering now recognizes a SETcc
into a register it just saw zeroed) the arm64 loop head is a single
CSET, each stream's carry add a single CSINC, and the loop-bottom test a
plain TST: six instructions fewer per iteration.

Validated: go vet on amd64 and arm64; huff0 tests on both (arm64 under
qemu-user); FuzzCompress (91s) and FuzzDecompress1x (46s) on amd64.

When a block is not marked as the final block it should be possible to read 10 further bits ahead without breaking the promise of not overreading.

entries.subject: flate: speed up writeTokens (#1218)
entries.message:
flate: speed up writeTokens (#1218)

Backport of https://go.dev/cl/829565 (golang/go#81398).

Rework the token writing loop to flush whole bytes from the bit
accumulator unconditionally after every iteration instead of testing
whether 48 bits have accumulated after every code. The old test was a
data dependent, poorly predicted branch; the new store, shift and add
are branch free. Since at most 7 bits are pending at the top of each
iteration, up to three literals (max 45 bits) or a complete match
(max 48 bits) fit into the accumulator without intermediate flushes.

Length codes and their extra bits, and offset codes and their extra
bits, are now merged into the accumulator with a single shift/or each.
A combined length table replaces three separate table lookups per
match, and offsetCombined now covers all offset codes so the extra bit
check can go away. lengthCode, lengthExtraBitsMinCode and
offsetExtraBitsMinCode are no longer used and are removed.

The output buffer is now written with unconditional 8-byte stores, so
tie its size to bufferFlushSize and document the slack that is needed.
The size is unchanged at 264 bytes, which is already the required
bufferFlushSize+7+8 rounded up to a multiple of 8.

The output is byte-identical.

NOTE on the Huffman-only rows below (PR/*/Huffman): those two numbers are a
code-layout artifact, not a real improvement, and should be read as 0%.
writeTokens is never executed at level -2 -- storeHuff calls only
writeBlockHuff, and writeTokens has zero profile samples there. This CL
shrinks writeTokens from 2112 to 1472 bytes, which pulls writeBlockHuff 416
bytes earlier in .text and changes its 64-byte alignment. writeBlockHuff's
disassembly is instruction-identical before and after, and the
huffmanBitWriter layout is unchanged (1360 bytes, same field offsets), so the
delta is purely placement. Inserting dead, never-called padding functions
before writeBlockHuff on master reproduces the whole effect with no source
change on the Huffman path; applying only this CL's table changes while
keeping the old writeTokens gives -0.17%.

Excluding those two rows, the geomean is +3.4% rather than +4.6%. The level
1-7 wins are real: writeTokens is on those paths.

Huffman-only throughput in this package swings 5-10% with code placement, so
treat any single-build Huffman-only measurement here below ~10% as unreliable.

* zstd: avoid racing MaxDecodedSize write on shared dict litEnc

Treeless literal decode wrote MaxDecodedSize on hist.huffTree, which
aliases dict.litEnc for trained dictionaries. Concurrent DecodeAll then
raced. Decoder.Decompress* already sizes via cap(dst), so drop the write.

Fixes #1180

Signed-off-by: zanarelli <zanarelli.dev@gmail.com>

* zstd: apply go fix to dict_test.go

Modernizes the alphabet-building loop in
TestSharedDecoderTrainedDictRace to a range-over-int loop, as flagged
by go fix and required by the build-special CI check.

Signed-off-by: zanarelli <zanarelli.dev@gmail.com>

entries.subject: zstd: close most of the decode gap to libzstd on real corpora (#1232)
entries.message:
zstd: close most of the decode gap to libzstd on real corpora (#1232)

* zstd: keep literal slack for treeless literal sections

A treeless literals section (Huffman table reused from the previous
block) was decoded into literalBuf[:0:litRegenSize] and kept that
capacity. The compressed-literals case re-slices to literalBuf to regain
the compressedBlockOverAlloc bytes past the end; the treeless case did
not, so useSafeDecodeSync saw no literal slack and sent every block that
reused a table to the bounds-exact decodeSync_safe loop.

The reference encoder reuses tables often. In the zstd -19 files from
klauspost.com/files/compress, as provided, the safe loop ran for 99% of
gob-stream's blocks, 85% of github-ranks-backup's, 62% of
sofia-air-quality's, 42% of cockroach's, 28% of nyc-taxi's and 5% of
apache's. After this change none do. Frames from this package's encoder
were not affected, since it rarely emits treeless sections.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01JsKM9Z6WCqNNFCZhjGHJcM

* zstd: stream synchronously through a history ring instead of sliding

With WithDecoderConcurrency(1), the Reader kept history in one buffer of
window plus 1 MiB (lowmem, the default) and, once free space fell to a
block, moved the whole window down. With an 8 MiB window that is an
8 MiB memmove per ~1 MiB of output: 22.8 GB moved to stream the 2.5 GB
apache.log from klauspost.com/files/compress, 75% of decode time.

Keep history in a ring of window plus two blocks of space, as the
reference decoder does. Each block is written at the current position
with its output capped to one block of space; when the next block would
not fit, the lap just written becomes ext and writing restarts at the
front. decodeSync already takes the history preceding out as a separate
slice, so ext is passed there and matches that start in the previous lap
continue into the current one. Nothing is moved, and the ring is smaller
than the lowmem buffer for windows above 256 KiB.

Block space and the space checks in decodeSyncSimple/useSafeDecodeSync
use the frame's maximum block size, min(window, 128 KiB), rather than
128 KiB, so small-window streams also reach the assembly.

The decodeSync "bigger than current history" errors now report bytes
produced by the current block without the history slice. That is what
DecodeAll and the Reader both reported before, since the slice was
always empty on those paths; TestDecoderRegression compares the two.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01JsKM9Z6WCqNNFCZhjGHJcM

* zstd: copy overlapping matches in 16-byte blocks when the offset allows

The assembly copied every overlapping match (length > offset) one byte
per iteration. With an offset of at least 16, each 16-byte block reads
only bytes that earlier blocks have already written, so these matches
can be copied like non-overlapping ones; the reference decoder does the
same and only special-cases offsets below 16.

Repeated content is mostly long overlapping matches at large offsets:
64% of html_x_4's output and 27-30% of apache.log's comes from them,
while shorter overlapping offsets are under 1% of any corpus measured.
DecodeAll as a share of libzstd's speed, pinned builds, 200 MB slices of
klauspost.com/files/compress plus the benchdecoder files:

                  html_x_4     apache -19   all real (geomean)
  Graviton5        37 ->  99%   59 -> 87%    84 -> 91%
  Graviton4        38 -> 100%   62 -> 85%    82 -> 88%
  Zen 4            37 ->  91%   67 -> 93%    87 -> 94%
  Sapphire Rapids  38 ->  92%   72 -> 89%    85 -> 90%
  Neoverse N1      31 ->  76%   54 -> 77%    71 -> 75%

The fast variant reuses the 16-byte copy loop and its 15-byte overrun;
the bounds-exact variant copies whole blocks and finishes byte by byte.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01JsKM9Z6WCqNNFCZhjGHJcM

* zstd: hash DecodeAll output block by block

runDecoder decoded the whole frame and then ran xxhash over all of it,
so for a large frame the checksum pass read the output back from memory
after it had left the cache. Hash each block's output as soon as it is
decoded instead, as the streaming decoder and the reference decoder do.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01JsKM9Z6WCqNNFCZhjGHJcM

* zstd: tighten the ring and overlap tests (review)

TestDecodeOverlappingMatches appended tail%period bytes, so a tail equal
to a multiple of the period appended nothing; append exactly tail bytes.

TestStreamRingWraps only compared output, so it did not show that
matches near the full window distance reach the decoder. Add an input
that repeats a random chunk of 15/16 of the window: it can only compress
through matches at that distance, and the test now requires it to shrink
to under half its size (45%, 46% and 15% for 1 KiB, 64 KiB and 1 MiB
windows).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01JsKM9Z6WCqNNFCZhjGHJcM

* zstd: use the history ring in the concurrent stream decoder

With the default concurrency the Reader's execute goroutine kept history
in window + 1 MiB (lowmem) and history.append moved the whole window down
whenever free space ran out, the same slide the synchronous path had.
With an 8 MiB window that is an 8 MiB memmove per ~1 MiB of output; on
Graviton5 it was 37% of CPU streaming klauspost.com's gob-stream and JSON
files, leaving the concurrent Reader slower than the synchronous one.

Execute sequences directly into the history ring, passing the previous
lap as history as decodeCompressed does, then copy the block's output to
its buffer. That keeps one copy per output byte, as before, without the
slide. Raw and RLE blocks append to the ring too, and the ring is kept
across Reset. history.append and allocFrameBuffer are no longer used and
are removed, and the "Last block" message is now debug-only.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01JsKM9Z6WCqNNFCZhjGHJcM

* zstd: test overlapping matches on the concurrent and two-pass paths

TestDecodeOverlappingMatches only reached decodeSync. The same copy change
is in executeSimple, which the concurrent Reader uses and, since #1212, so
does the two-pass DecodeAll path. Run each input through both, too.
Changing executeSimple's threshold from 16 to 8 now fails 30 of the
subtests on amd64; before, none failed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* zstd: remove unreachable output allocation from runDecoder

runDecoder set d.history.b = dst before the block that grew dst when
cap(dst) < maxSyncLen, so if it ran it copied the output for nothing:
decoding kept appending to the old buffer and the copy was dropped.

It cannot run. DecodeAll, the only caller, grows dst to at least
len(dst)+FrameContentSize+compressedBlockOverAlloc under the same
condition (known content size, !limitToCap), which is maxSyncLen plus the
slack. A panic planted in it was never reached by the zstd tests with and
without noasm or by 300000 FuzzDecodeAll executions.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entries.subject: docs: Add AGENTS.md (#1238)
entries.message:
docs: Add AGENTS.md (#1238)

* Add AGENTS.md

Conventions and traps for people and coding agents changing the
repository: generated assembly and the avo fork, the PCALIGN label hazard,
assembly calls, build tags, checks and fuzzing before sending a change,
where tests go, what counts as evidence for a performance claim, and
pull-request conventions.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* AGENTS.md: swap which build runs first each round

Alternating A and B still gives one of them the same slot every round;
swapping the order each round keeps warm-up and slot effects off both.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* AGENTS.md: reflow the benchmark alternation bullet

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* AGENTS.md: registers with fixed roles survive calls

Go's ABI has no callee-saved registers, but the stack and frame pointers
and the goroutine register keep their roles across a call. Say so, as the
ABI document does, while keeping the rule to spill everything else.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* AGENTS.md: address review

- Drop the bullet on calling Go from assembly; it is too specific here.
- Vet code for every platform it targets instead of naming arm64, and test
  on every architecture whose assembly changed.
- Check `go fix -diff ./...`.
- Move the assembly section to the end; the others are more general.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* gzhttp: apply go fix

Use slices.Backward, so `go fix -diff ./...` reports nothing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entries.message:
flate: restructure matchLen to avoid bounds checks (#1216)

Backport of https://go.dev/cl/829564 (golang/go#81398).

The load-helper half of the upstream CL does not apply here:
internal/le's Load32/Load64 already use unsafe pointer arithmetic on
amd64, arm64, ppc64le and riscv64, so there are no per-byte bounds
checks to remove, and the !unsafe fallback goes through encoding/binary,
which already compiles to a single combined load.

Only the matchLen restructuring is carried over: truncate b to the
length of a up front and reslice both as the comparison advances, so
the loop condition proves every load in bounds and the byte-at-a-time
tail loses its bounds check on b[i].

The output is byte-identical.

As predicted from the above, this is performance neutral on the default
build, where the loads are already unchecked: geomean +0.1%, every
benchmark within noise. The table below is the default build.

entries.subject: zstd: improve header decoder (#476)
entries.message:
zstd: improve header decoder (#476)

Changes made:
* Add Header.HeaderSize to track the actual size of the header.
The header is variable length, so providing this information allows
the caller to do other low-level tasks, such as determining whether
the entirety of a zstandard frame is a single segment block.
* Add Header.Skippable{ID,Size} to make the Header type more
useful for extracting data from metadata frames (see #459).
* Re-arrange fields in Header to better match the order
these appear in RFC 8478.

Add stateless gzip/deflate (#176)

* Add stateless gzip/deflate

StatelessCompression will do compression but without maintaining any state between Write calls.

There will be no memory kept between Write calls, but compression and speed will be suboptimal.

Because of this, the size of actual Write calls will affect output size.

entries.subject: Add WithNoEntropyCompression to zstd (#187)
entries.message:
Add WithNoEntropyCompression to zstd (#187)

WithNoEntropyCompression will always skip entropy compression of literals.
This can be useful if content has matches, but unlikely to benefit from entropy compression.
Usually the slight speed improvement is not worth enabling this.
